strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem: continual online adaptation of interactive medical image segmentation models under post-deployment distribution shift.
The method is simple and potentially deployable: a two-stage update procedure plus Gaussian Point Loss avoids complex teacher-student machinery and appears computationally cheaper than TSCA/IA+SA.
Empirical scope is reasonably broad, covering 5 fundus datasets and 4 brain MRI datasets, including modality and pathology shifts.
The comparisons mostly use the same base interactive model, which makes the online adaptation comparison with TSCA and IA+SA more controlled.
Results show consistent and sometimes large gains, especially for strong shifts such as BRATS T1/T1c and ATLAS T1, and ablations support the contribution of the two stages and GPL.
weaknesses: The central supervision signal is the model's own final prediction after simulated user clicks, treated as pseudo ground truth. The paper does not sufficiently analyze failure modes when this final prediction is wrong, which is likely under severe shifts and clinically important cases.

The evaluation relies on simulated clicks generated using ground-truth error regions. This is standard but weakens claims about real user interaction, since real clinicians may click differently, inconsistently, or stop before 10 clicks.

Novelty is moderate: local Gaussian-weighted losses around clicks and two-stage self-training are reasonable but incremental relative to prior interactive segmentation adaptation and click-based correction objectives.

Baselines are limited. The paper compares mainly to IA+SA and TSCA, with only a narrow MedSAM adapter comparison; stronger current interactive medical segmentation methods and test-time adaptation/self-training baselines are missing.

Important adaptation details are underspecified or underanalyzed, including sequence ordering sensitivity, accumulation of errors over long streams, catastrophic degradation on mixed distributions, runtime/memory costs, and hyperparameter sensitivity for beta, sigma, learning rate, and number of updates.
Statistical evidence is incomplete: only some results are averaged over three runs, standard deviations/confidence intervals are absent from the tables, and significance of improvements is unclear.
The use of a private TBI dataset and the promise that code/models will be released later limit reproducibility at submission time.

Clinical claims are somewhat stronger than the evidence. The paper does not evaluate real clinician-in-the-loop use, annotation burden, privacy/security implications of online learning from deployment data, or safeguards against harmful adaptation.

strengths: The paper targets a practically relevant problem: adapting interactive medical image segmentation models after deployment using user corrections under distribution shift.
The proposed method is simple and computationally lightweight, combining pseudo-label distillation from multi-click predictions with a Gaussian-weighted click loss.
Experiments cover multiple datasets across fundus imaging and brain MRI, including modality and pathology shifts, and compare against two relevant continuous-adaptation baselines.
The reported gains are often substantial, especially for cross-modality brain MRI and some fundus cup segmentation settings.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited. The main ingredients are relatively incremental: self-training/distillation from corrected predictions, Gaussian-weighted supervision around clicks, and a two-stage fine-tuning schedule. The paper does not sufficiently distinguish the contribution from prior interactive adaptation and click-based loss formulations.

The evaluation relies entirely on simulated user clicks derived from ground-truth error regions. This is a major limitation for a paper whose motivation is real clinical interaction, because the click policy may strongly favor the proposed adaptation mechanism and may not reflect clinician behavior, time constraints, or correction patterns.

The method uses the model's own final prediction after 10 simulated clicks as pseudo-ground truth. The paper does not analyze when this pseudo-label is wrong, how errors accumulate during continuous adaptation, or how robust the approach is to noisy or inconsistent user feedback.

Baselines are insufficient for a top-tier AI venue. The comparison is mainly against IA+SA and TSCA, with only limited use of MedSAM Adapter. There is no broad comparison to modern test-time adaptation, self-training, continual adaptation, or stronger interactive segmentation methods.

Experimental protocol details are under-specified. The ordering of online test sequences, sensitivity to order, number of adaptation epochs/steps, memory/computation cost, hyperparameter tuning procedure, and statistical significance are not adequately reported.

The MRI evaluation is clinically weak: it uses only the 2D slice with the largest lesion area per case and merges labels, which substantially simplifies the segmentation task and limits conclusions about real volumetric medical image segmentation.

A private TBI dataset is used without sufficient detail, limiting reproducibility. Code and models are only promised after publication, and several implementation choices needed to reproduce the method are missing.

The ablation study is narrow and mostly qualitative from plots. It does not convincingly isolate the contribution of GPL, the two-stage schedule, pseudo-label quality, number of clicks, or hyperparameters across the diverse datasets.

Claims about clinical reliability and deployment are stronger than the evidence. There is no real-user study, no failure-case analysis, no safety discussion, and no assessment of harmful adaptation under wrong corrections or outlier cases.
Presentation quality is below expectation, with formatting issues, placeholder author text, unclear notation, and imprecise descriptions of the optimization and click-generation procedures.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem: continuous post-deployment adaptation of interactive medical image segmentation models under distribution shift.
The proposed method is simple and clinically plausible in spirit: it reuses user corrections, adds a Gaussian-weighted point loss around clicks, and requires only two backpropagation steps per image.
Evaluation spans a reasonably broad set of medical segmentation shifts, including 5 fundus datasets and multiple brain MRI modality/pathology shifts.
Comparisons to IA+SA and TSCA are reasonably controlled by using the same base interactive model and learning rates, which makes the reported gains more interpretable.
Results are consistently positive, especially under larger shifts such as BRATS FLAIR to T1/T1c and ATLAS T1, where the improvements over the frozen model and TSCA are substantial.
The ablation study supports the value of the two-stage adaptation procedure and the Gaussian Point Loss, rather than only showing end-to-end gains.
weaknesses: The interaction process is entirely simulated, so the core claim of learning from user interaction in clinical workflows is only indirectly supported; real users or at least stronger click-simulation sensitivity analyses would make the evidence more convincing.

Novelty is moderate: the work combines online self-training from corrected predictions with a local Gaussian-weighted click loss, but the conceptual distance from prior continuous adaptation and point-supervised losses is not very large.

The pseudo-ground-truth construction depends on the base model's final prediction after simulated clicks, which may propagate systematic errors; the paper does not sufficiently analyze failure cases or when adaptation could degrade over long sequences.

Reproducibility is incomplete: code is only promised after publication, one dataset is private, and important implementation details such as sequence ordering, number of optimization steps, memory/state handling, and hyperparameter sensitivity are under-specified.
Statistical reporting is limited. Most tables lack standard deviations, confidence intervals, significance tests, or analysis across different stream orders, despite the online nature of the method.

The brain MRI setup uses only the 2D slice with largest lesion area and merges labels, which simplifies the clinical segmentation problem and may overstate applicability to full volumetric medical workflows.

The comparison set is somewhat narrow. The paper includes TSCA/IA+SA and a MedSAM adapter in one setting, but does not deeply compare against stronger modern promptable medical segmentation adaptation strategies or test-time adaptation baselines.
Claims about simplicity and reliability would be stronger with runtime, memory, latency, and robustness analyses, since online backpropagation after every image may matter in deployment.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem: adapting interactive medical segmentation models under deployment-time distribution shift using user corrections.
The proposed OAIMS framework is simple and computationally light, with a clear separation between post-interaction and mid-interaction adaptation.
Empirical coverage is fairly broad, spanning fundus and brain MRI datasets, multiple shifts across scanners/modalities/pathologies, and several online adaptation baselines.
Results are consistently strong, especially for MRI modality shifts where reported gains over IA+SA and TSCA are substantial.
The paper includes useful ablations for PI/MI components, the CCG loss design, hyperparameters, fewer-click settings, mixed-domain adaptation, and robustness to poor pseudo-labels or noisy clicks.
weaknesses: The evaluation relies entirely on simulated clicks generated from ground truth, which weakens the clinical realism of the claims. No real user study or annotation-time analysis is provided.

The central assumption that final user-refined model outputs are reliable pseudo-ground-truth is only indirectly tested; in the experiments, corrections are oracle-simulated rather than produced by clinicians.

Novelty is moderate: Gaussian-weighted click losses and online/pseudo-label adaptation are plausible extensions of prior interactive segmentation and continuous adaptation methods, rather than a clearly new paradigm.
The MRI evaluation is simplified to 2D slices with the largest lesion area and often merges multiclass labels into binary segmentation, limiting conclusions about full clinical 3D workflows.

Reproducibility is incomplete: code and pretrained models are only promised after publication, and some implementation details such as sequence ordering, dataset preprocessing, exact splits for non-BRATS datasets, and optimization settings are not fully specified in the main paper.

Statistical uncertainty is limited: most main tables report point estimates without confidence intervals or significance tests, despite sequential online adaptation being potentially sensitive to ordering and random seeds.

The comparison to SAM/Med-SA is not very informative because it is frozen at test time and appears much weaker than the U-Net backbone; stronger promptable medical segmentation baselines or adapted foundation models would improve positioning.

Several claims about real-world practicality and clinical workflow are stronger than the evidence, since latency is measured but human interaction quality, user burden, and failure modes in real clinical use are not evaluated.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: adapting interactive medical image segmentation models under distribution shift, where clinician feedback could plausibly provide useful online supervision.
The proposed OAIMS framework is clearly organized into pretraining, mid-interaction adaptation, and post-interaction adaptation, and the Click-Centered Gaussian loss is intuitive.
The empirical section is fairly broad in dataset coverage, spanning fundus images and several brain MRI datasets/modalities, with comparisons to ICNN, IA+SA, TSCA, and Med-SA.
The paper includes useful ablations for PI/MI components, CCG design choices, hyperparameters, noisy clicks, fewer-click settings, mixed-domain streams, and source-like data.
weaknesses: The core contribution is incremental. The method largely combines existing ideas: interactive segmentation with click maps, pseudo-label/self-training, online test-time updates, and localized click-weighted losses. The paper does not convincingly establish a substantial conceptual advance beyond prior online interactive segmentation methods such as IA+SA and TSCA.

The evaluation is heavily simulation-based. User clicks are generated from ground-truth error regions, which is standard for some interactive segmentation benchmarks but weak support for clinical usability claims. No real clinician interaction study is provided, despite repeated claims about clinical workflows.

The main assumption that the final interactive prediction is reliable pseudo-ground truth is not adequately validated in realistic settings. The robustness experiments are helpful but still synthetic and do not replace evidence from human-corrected masks or real annotation behavior.

The MRI evaluation is artificially simplified: 3D scans are reduced to the 2D slice with the largest lesion area, and multi-class lesions are merged into binary labels. This substantially limits the clinical and technical significance of the reported gains.

The paper’s claims of broad applicability and practical deployment are stronger than the evidence. Latency is reported, but memory, cumulative update stability over longer deployment, model drift, quality control, and failure detection are not studied sufficiently.

Baselines are limited for a top-tier AI venue. The comparison focuses on a small set of interactive adaptation methods and a frozen Med-SA model, but does not include stronger or more recent medical foundation-model adaptation, test-time adaptation, continual/online segmentation, or nnU-Net style baselines under matched interactive protocols.

Some experimental reporting is incomplete. Many results lack confidence intervals or statistical significance tests; only some ablations mention three seeds. Dataset sizes, preprocessing, optimizer details, learning rates, stopping/update details, and exact prompt/click simulation choices are not all sufficiently clear for reproduction.

The strongest gains occur under large distribution shifts where the base model is very weak, but the paper does not fully disentangle whether improvements come from the proposed CCG loss, repeated gradient updates on pseudo-labels, or the particular ground-truth-driven click simulator.
Reproducibility is not yet strong: code and pretrained models are only promised upon publication, and important implementation details are relegated to high-level algorithm descriptions.
The writing is understandable but sometimes overstates impact, e.g. claims of transformative clinical potential and clinician-ready deployment are not justified by the presented evidence.

strengths: The paper addresses a clear and practically important problem: making interactive medical image segmentation models adapt online under distribution shift using user corrections. This is well motivated for clinical deployment, where scanner, site, modality, and pathology shifts are common.

The proposed framework is simple and coherent. The separation into post-interaction adaptation and mid-interaction adaptation is intuitive, and the Click-Centered Gaussian loss is a sensible way to use more information than a single clicked pixel while still focusing learning around user-provided corrections.

The empirical evaluation is fairly broad, covering fundus datasets and several brain MRI modality/pathology shifts. The reported gains over ICNN, IA+SA, TSCA, and Med-SA are often large, especially for challenging MRI shifts such as BraTS FLAIR to T1/T1c and ATLAS.

The ablation studies are useful and support the main design choices: PI and MI are both examined, the CCG loss components are ablated, hyperparameters are explored, and robustness to noisy clicks, poor pseudo-labels, many clicks, and mixed-domain image streams is investigated.
The method appears computationally practical, with low reported adaptation latency on both GPU and CPU, which is important for an interactive workflow.
The paper is generally understandable and the algorithmic description in the appendix makes the training and online adaptation procedure reasonably clear.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate rather than strong. The method combines online adaptation from corrections, pseudo-labeling from corrected outputs, and a localized click-weighted loss; these are useful engineering choices, but the conceptual advance over prior interactive adaptation methods such as IA+SA and TSCA could be positioned more sharply.

The evaluation relies entirely on simulated clicks. This is common, but it is a major limitation for a clinical interactive segmentation paper, since real users may click differently, stop at different points, and provide imperfect corrections in ways not captured by the simulator.

The experiments reduce 3D MRI volumes to 2D slices with the largest lesion area and merge lesion subclasses into binary labels. This simplifies the task and limits evidence that the method will work in realistic 3D clinical segmentation workflows.

The pseudo-ground-truth assumption is central but not fully validated with real corrected masks. Since the final model output after simulated interactions is treated as a training target, the method’s behavior may differ when users are satisfied with masks that contain systematic errors or when corrections are sparse and subjective.

The comparison to stronger modern medical segmentation backbones is limited. Med-SA is included but performs poorly, and most experiments use a U-Net-style ICNN backbone; it remains unclear how well the method transfers to stronger 2D/3D nnU-Net variants or promptable foundation models.

Reporting could be more rigorous statistically. Many tables provide point estimates, while variance, confidence intervals, significance testing, and sensitivity to image ordering are limited or only partially addressed.

Reproducibility is incomplete at submission time: code and pretrained models are promised only upon publication, and implementation details such as optimization settings during adaptation, exact learning rates, preprocessing, and hardware measurement protocol need more complete specification in the main paper.
